blocks.x: Key definitions

Cell The basic structural and functional unit of all living organisms — the smallest unit of life capable of independently performing the functions of life (growth, reproduction, response to stimuli, metabolism).

Cell Theory A unifying framework stating that (1) all living things are composed of one or more cells, (2) the cell is the basic unit of structure and organization in organisms, and (3) cells arise only from pre-existing cells, through cell division.
Prokaryotic cell A cell that lacks a membrane-bound nucleus and lacks complex, membrane-bound organelles; its DNA lies free in the cytoplasm.
Eukaryotic cell A cell that possesses a true, membrane-bound nucleus and a variety of membrane-bound organelles that compartmentalize its functions.
The Cell & Cell Theory→ Prokaryotes vs Eukaryotes→ Cell Size, Shape & SA:V Ratio→ Cytoplasmic Organelles (next topic)

sections.title: The three tenets of Cell Theory

blocks.x: Foundations of cell biology
Every living thing, from a single bacterium to a whale, is built from cells — and every cell traces back to a pre-existing cell.

The cell — smallest unit of life A cell is the smallest unit of life capable of independently performing all the functions of life. Nothing smaller than a cell can, on its own, grow, reproduce, process information, respond to stimuli, and carry out the chemical reactions that define living matter.
The three tenets of Cell Theory

items: 1All living things are composed of one or more cells. Whether an organism is unicellular (one cell) or multicellular (many cells), the cell is its fundamental building block.
2The cell is the basic unit of structure and organization in organisms. Tissues, organs and whole organisms are all built up from cells as the smallest organized living unit.
3Cells arise only from pre-existing cells, via cell division. Life does not spontaneously generate from non-living matter — every new cell is produced by the division of a parent cell.

blocks.x: Pre-existing cell→ Cell division→ New cell(s)→ Tissues & organisms
Abilities that define a living cell
Living cells share a set of defining abilities. Even the simplest single-celled (unicellular) organisms exhibit all of the major properties of life:

items: ✓Grow — cells increase in size and biomass by synthesizing new cellular material.
✓Reproduce — cells copy their genetic material and divide to produce new cells.
✓Process information — cells store, read and use genetic information to direct their own activities.
✓Respond to stimuli — cells detect and react to changes in their internal and external environment.
✓Carry out chemical reactions — cells run the metabolic reactions (synthesis and breakdown of molecules) that sustain life.

blocks.x: General functions of the cell

c: Chemical reactions are confined within specialized structures inside the cell, keeping incompatible processes separated and efficient.
The cell regulates the inflow and outflow of materials — nutrients in, waste and products out — across its boundary.
The cell uses its genetic material (DNA) to direct and coordinate all of its activities.
The continuity of life originates from the cell — new cells (and new organisms) arise only from existing cells.

blocks.x: Cellular diversity in the human body

~100 trillion cells, ~200 cell types The human body contains an estimated 100 trillion (100,000,000,000,000) cells, organized into roughly 200 different cell types (e.g. neurons, red blood cells, muscle cells, epithelial cells). Cells vary widely in size and shape, and this variation is closely related to the specific function each cell type performs.
Prokaryotic vs eukaryotic cells — the big split

Despite this diversity, every cell on Earth falls into one of two fundamental categories: prokaryotic cells (cells without a nucleus) and eukaryotic cells (cells with a nucleus). This distinction, explored in depth in the next tab, is the single most important dividing line in cell biology.
The two fundamental cell categories
Every cell is either prokaryotic (no nucleus) or eukaryotic (true nucleus) — a distinction that runs through DNA packaging, cell wall chemistry and internal organization.
Prokaryotic

Lacks a membrane-bound nucleus and lacks complex, membrane-bound organelles. DNA lies free in the cytoplasm, in a region called the nucleoid, rather than being enclosed in a nuclear envelope. Includes Bacteria and Archaea.
Eukaryotic
Possesses a true, membrane-bound nucleus that encloses its DNA, plus a variety of other membrane-bound organelles that compartmentalize specific cellular functions.
How prokaryotes differ from eukaryotes

items: 1DNA packaging — prokaryotes have no nucleus, and their DNA is not wrapped around histones (the DNA-packaging proteins eukaryotes use); it lies free in the cytoplasm's nucleoid region.
2Cell wall makeup — prokaryotic Bacteria have cell walls made of peptidoglycan; prokaryotic Archaea have tough walls made of other, distinct chemicals (not peptidoglycan).
3Internal structures — prokaryotes have no complex, membrane-bound organelles (no nucleus, mitochondria, ER, Golgi, etc.), unlike the compartmentalized interior of eukaryotic cells.

blocks.x: Prokaryotic vs Eukaryotic cells — comparison table

c: Present — e.g. mitochondria, ER, Golgi apparatus

blocks.x: Simpler organization, smaller size

Prokaryotic form and function Prokaryotic cells have a simpler internal organization than eukaryotic cells — they lack the internal membrane systems and compartments found in eukaryotes. They are also generally smaller in cell size than eukaryotic cells, which (as the next tab shows) helps them maintain an efficient surface-area-to-volume ratio.

blocks.x: Geometry meets biology
Why is almost every cell microscopic? The answer is geometric — as a cell grows, its volume outpaces its surface area, choking off diffusion.
Factors that determine cell shape
The shape of a cell depends on several factors acting together:

items: 1Surface tension and viscosity of the cytoplasm — the physical properties of the cell's internal fluid help set its outer shape.
2Mechanical action of adjoining cells — pressure and contact from neighboring cells can flatten or reshape a cell (e.g. in tightly packed tissue).
3Rigidity of the cell membrane — a stiffer membrane (or cell wall) holds a more fixed shape; a flexible membrane allows more variable shapes.
4Functional adaptation — a cell's shape is often adapted to the specific function it performs (e.g. the elongated shape of a nerve cell, or the biconcave disc of a red blood cell).

blocks.x: Surface-area-to-volume (SA:V) ratio

Surface-area-to-volume (SA:V) ratio The ratio of a cell's outer surface area (through which nutrients, gases and wastes diffuse) to its volume (which determines its metabolic demand). As a cell gets larger, its volume grows faster than its surface area, so the SA:V ratio falls.
SA:V ratio for a cube-shaped cell as it grows

As the cube's side length doubles from 1 cm → 2 cm → 4 cm, volume grows cubically (1 cm³ → 8 cm³ → 64 cm³) while total surface area grows only squarely (6 cm² → 24 cm² → 96 cm²). The result: the SA:V ratio falls steadily — 6 cm⁻¹ → 3 cm⁻¹ → 1.5 cm⁻¹ — even though the cell has gotten much bigger.
Why most cells stay microscopic

The SA:V limit on cell size Cells need a high SA:V ratio for efficient diffusion of nutrients, gases and waste across the plasma membrane, relative to their metabolic demand (which scales with volume). If a cell grows too large, its surface area can no longer keep pace with its volume's metabolic needs — diffusion becomes too slow to supply the cell's interior or remove its waste. This geometric constraint is a major reason most cells remain microscopic.
Cell size ↑→ Volume ↑↑↑ (cubic)→ Surface area ↑↑ (square)→ SA:V ↓→ Diffusion limited
